title: Three Questions to Ask After Every Conversation, According to Author Kate Murphy e-murphy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. distills a listening framework from Kate Murphy's book You're Not Listening into three questions leaders and educators can ask themselves after any conversation: what did I learn about that person, what was most concerning to them, and how did they feel about what we discussed. He argues that listening is an undervalued discipline — it earns no TED talks or news interviews — yet is foundational to loving a conversation partner well, whether in a team meeting, a parent-teacher conference, or a hallway chat with a colleague. Stuart applies the three questions across three professional contexts (staff meetings, parent conferences, and colleague conversations), suggesting they can redirect conversations away from complaining and toward more productive ends. He closes by offering a simple printable tracker for logging five people listened to each day.
points: Murphy's three questions (what did I learn, what concerned them, how did they feel) are framed as a portable self-check for listening quality across team meetings, parent conferences, and colleague conversations.
Stuart explicitly ties failure to answer any of the three questions to a specific listening failure: not attending, lacking empathy, or ignoring emotion.
He positions the framework as a leadership tool for staff and team interactions, not just a classroom technique, applying it first to team meetings.
The piece offers a concrete habit-tracker — a printable sheet for five people listened to per day — to make the practice measurable rather than aspirational.
quotes: It doesn't get much glory — the million-view TED talks aren't videos of people listening; the folks who get interviewed on the morning news aren't being interviewed for their skill in listening.
What did I just learn about that person? If you can't answer this, you either weren't listening or you didn't give your conversation partner a chance to talk.
What was most concerning to that person? If you can't answer this, you weren't very empathetic, and it's unlikely that they felt listened to.
During a team meeting, be it remote or in-person: Did I learn anything about my teammates? Did I pick up on what they're concerned about? Did I attend to their emotions?
My hunch is that Murphy's questions will help me focus on the person I'm speaking with and improve the outcomes of my conversations.
I'm curious to see how just attending to these three questions helps guide conversations away from complaint-land and toward more productive things.
